questions.explanation: „Meiner Meinung nach“ opens an opinion. „Nach“ comes after the noun here, which is unusual — the phrase is worth learning whole rather than built.

questions.stem: What does „ich finde“ mean in an opinion?
questions.explanation: „Ich finde, dass …“ is the everyday way to give an opinion, more common in speech than „ich denke“. Literally 'I find', but it means 'I think'.
„Weil“ gives a reason and sends its verb to the end of the clause. „Während“ is 'while' and „obwohl“ is 'although' — both do the same thing to the word order.
„Trotzdem“ marks a contrast, like „dennoch“. „Deshalb“ means therefore and points the other way, so mixing them reverses the logic of a sentence.
„Die Arbeit“ is work. „Der Arbeiter“ is a worker and „arbeiten“ is the verb — a family of words worth learning together.
„Aktuell“ means current or up-to-date. English 'actual' is „tatsächlich“. It is the same false friend German shares with French, and it changes the meaning of a whole sentence.
„Sensibel“ means sensitive. English 'sensible' is „vernünftig“. Because the word exists in both languages with different meanings, it slips past a reader who is not watching for it.
„Das Handy“ is a mobile phone — an English-looking word that English does not use this way. Germans call these words Scheinanglizismen, borrowed shapes with invented meanings.

questions.stem: Which phrase best introduces a counter-argument?
questions.explanation: „Auf der anderen Seite“ is 'on the other hand'. The others structure an argument too, but do different jobs: giving an example, summing up, and opening a first point.

questions.stem: What does „Ich bin damit einverstanden“ mean?
questions.explanation: „Einverstanden sein“ is to agree. „Ich verstehe“ means 'I understand', which is a different claim and the near-miss here.

questions.stem: What does „es kommt darauf an“ mean?
questions.explanation: An idiom that cannot be worked out from its parts, and one of the most useful phrases in a discussion. Literally 'it comes upon it'.

options: To be happy about something past

„Umwelt“ is the environment and „-freundlich“ means friendly to it. German builds this kind of compound freely, so knowing the parts unlocks the whole word.

questions.stem: Which phrase means 'in my view, it is important that'?
options: Meiner Meinung nach ist es wichtig, dass
In meiner Meinung ist es wichtig, dass
Nach meine Meinung ist es wichtig, dass
Meine Meinung nach ist wichtig, dass
questions.explanation: „Meiner Meinung nach“ takes the dative and puts „nach“ after the noun. Translating 'in my opinion' word for word gives „in meiner Meinung“, which is not German.

questions.stem: Which sentence best expresses 'I would rather stay at home'?
options: Ich würde lieber zu Hause bleiben nicht
Ich bleibe gern zu Hause mehr
Ich möchte lieber zu Haus bleiben
questions.explanation: „Lieber“ is the comparative of „gern“ and does the work of 'would rather' on its own — no conditional needed. „Zu Hause“ means at home; „nach Hause“ means homewards.

questions.stem: Which sentence means 'the more I learn, the more I understand'?
options: Je mehr ich lerne, je mehr ich verstehe
Mehr ich lerne, mehr ich verstehe
Je mehr lerne ich, desto mehr ich verstehe
Je mehr ich lerne, desto mehr verstehe ich
questions.explanation: The pattern is „je … desto …“, and the second half inverts so the verb comes before the subject. Both halves have their own word order rule, which is what the wrong options miss.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I have been waiting for an hour'?
options: Ich bin eine Stunde am warten
Ich habe seit einer Stunde gewartet
questions.explanation: German keeps the present tense with „seit“ for something still going on, and „seit“ takes the dative — „einer Stunde“. English switches to a perfect form, and copying that implies the waiting has stopped.

questions.stem: Which best translates 'I miss my family'?
questions.explanation: „Vermissen“ works like the English verb, taking a direct object — unlike French, where the roles reverse. „Mir fehlt meine Familie“ is also correct German, but the option here negates it.

questions.stem: What does „doch“ add to a sentence like „Komm doch mit!“?
options: A negative, making it 'do not come'
A question, making it 'are you coming?'
Nothing; it is filler with no effect
A softening nudge, like 'do come along'
questions.explanation: „Doch“, „mal“, „ja“ and „eben“ are flavouring particles. They carry tone rather than meaning, English does the same job with intonation, and they are most of what makes German sound German.
